paras: The Douglas Club shooting was a fight between a party of white men and Black patrons at the Douglas Club, a Black resort at 147 West 28th Street in New York's Tenderloin, late on the night of August 12, 1910. According to the New-York Tribune, the fight began when one of the white visitors threw a whiskey bottle that struck a Black woman singer on the head, and three of the white men were shot before police cleared the club. Associated Press dispatches carried the story across the country as a "race riot," and two Black men connected with the club were held on charges of felonious assault.

The Tribune called the Douglas Club "one of the most frequented resorts of its kind in the Tenderloin." Shortly before midnight, by the Tribune's account, about a dozen white men drove up in four taxicabs, "shouting lustily," and took seats at the tables. The Associated Press gave a different reason for their visit: the white men, "mostly east side roughs," had gone to the resort in search of a Black man who had recently shot an East Side resident.

Inside, the Tribune reported, clashes with Black patrons were narrowly avoided several times before one of the white men threw a heavy whiskey bottle that hit a young Black woman who was singing. The wire described the trigger as "an insult offered a negress singer by a white man," and police, according to a German-language report printed in Baltimore, attributed the quarrel to a disparaging remark about the singer. Black men and women in the room rose in anger, bottles, glasses and chairs flew, and the Tribune said some Black patrons then drew razors and revolvers. The wire said more than thirty shots were fired and twenty others were more or less injured.

Three white men were shot: John McCarthy, an agent, and Joseph Cryons, both reported as 20 and wounded in the side and arm, and William Dehriens, 22. McCarthy was said to be dying and Cryons was in critical condition, and the wire added that a fourth man was said to have been shot and carried off by friends. Reserves from the West 30th Street station under Captain O'Brien then broke down the doors and cleared the club.

Police arrested Edmund Johnson, described as the proprietor, and Frank H. Berryman, the doorkeeper, both Black, and charged them with felonious assault after McCarthy and Cryons identified them at the hospital. The next day both men were held in $1,000 bail each in the Jefferson Market court. No arrest of any of the white men was reported, and the coverage does not show whether the wounded men survived or how the charges against Johnson and Berryman ended.

The New-York Tribune's local story ran under the headline "SHOOT WHITES IN RESORT" but carried the deck "WHITES STARTED BATTLE," placing the start of the fight on the visitors. Its narrative nonetheless treated the Black patrons' response as mock warfare, describing a "modern inferno" and white men caught "in the centre of a black hornets' nest."

The Associated Press dispatch ran on August 13 in papers from Maine to California, including the Daily Kennebec Journal, the Norwich Bulletin and the Los Angeles Herald, and weekly papers such as the Bamberg Herald of South Carolina reprinted it as late as August 18. Headline writers framed it as a racial clash, under titles such as "Race Riot in New York" and "Bloody, Deadly Riot of Whites and Blacks." Some overstated the toll: the Montgomery Advertiser's headline read "Three Die in Affray Between Whites and Negroes" and the Daily Missoulian's "Three Whites Killed in New York Resort," though their texts reported only wounds. All of the reports found appeared in white newspapers, including a German-language daily in Baltimore; no Black-press account of the fight was found.

Accounts differ on why the white men came: the Tribune presented them as a noisy party ending a night out, while the Associated Press called them "east side roughs" hunting a Black man who had shot an East Sider. They also differ on numbers, about a dozen whites against about a hundred Black patrons in the Tribune and sixty men of both races in the wire, and on the trigger, a thrown bottle in the Tribune and an insult or disparaging remark in the wire and police versions.

reader.title: Douglas Club shooting
bases: A party of white men entered a Black resort and, by the local account, one struck a Black woman singer with a thrown bottle, setting off a fight in which three of the whites were shot (A1, A2); casualties reported are white, so the case is borderline for anti-Black violence.

The New-York Tribune's local report and the independent Associated Press dispatch agree on the place, the three white men shot and the singer as the trigger (A1, A2, A3), and a German-language report adds a police version (A13).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune local report
accounts.gist: A noisy party of about a dozen white men started a free fight with about a hundred Black patrons when one threw a whiskey bottle that struck a Black woman singer; Black patrons fought back and drew razors and revolvers, and three whites were shot.

accounts.label: Associated Press wire
accounts.gist: Sixty men of both races fought after a white man insulted a Black woman singer; more than thirty shots were fired, three whites shot, a fourth said shot, twenty injured; the whites were east side roughs looking for a Black man who had shot an East Sider.

accounts.label: Police version (German-language report)
accounts.gist: Police said the quarrel arose from a white man's disparaging remark about the Black singer; the whites were said to be drunk; police said the wounded named Johnson and Berryman as the men who shot them.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed its story 'SHOOT WHITES IN RESORT' but 'WHITES STARTED BATTLE', and described the Black patrons' response in mock-battle language ('a black hornets' nest').
Wire papers headlined it 'RACE RIOT IN NEW YORK' and 'BLOODY, DEADLY RIOT OF WHITES AND BLACKS', with the insult to the 'negress singer' as cause.
The Montgomery Advertiser and Daily Missoulian headlines said three died or were killed although their texts reported only wounds.

info: Late at night on Friday 12 August 1910, running past midnight into 13 August
Douglas Club, a Black resort at No. 147 West 28th Street, in the Tenderloin, New York
A young Black woman singer struck on the head by a whiskey bottle thrown by a white man (Tribune); three white men shot: John McCarthy, Joseph Cryons, William Dehriens
None against the singer; the wire said the white men had come seeking the Black assailant of an East Sider recently shot
About a dozen white men who arrived in four taxicabs (Tribune), described by the wire as 'mostly east side roughs'; none named
Johnson and Berryman held in $1,000 bail each in Jefferson Market court on 13 August; no later outcome found
